source.title: Broken Latents: Studying SAEs and Feature Co-occurrence in Toy Models

record.file_problem: none; full post and comments are present
record.tranche_reason: The post tests toy SAE representations under feature co-occurrence and capacity changes, and refines the assumption that narrow SAEs cleanly represent parent features. Its results also compare a modified training loss with the standard objective.
record.gate_note: The post includes cited results from earlier work, which are not recorded as rows. The independent-feature experiments are included only where they provide a comparison for the co-occurrence tests. No experiment directly tests whether increasing dictionary size splits a coarse feature into geometrically close children that partition its inputs.
record.test_reason: Toy SAE experiments test whether co-occurring parent/child features yield clean latents across SAE widths (1 latent, undercomplete, overcomplete) and tied/untied architectures (V4). They also compare the standard objective with a custom auxiliary loss and argue against the Matryoshka assumption that narrow SAEs learn clean parent latents (V6). The post is a follow-up by an original-source author but is not itself an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add: the authors argue the core Matryoshka assumption (narrow SAEs learn clean parent latents) is not strictly true, so Matryoshka SAEs should not be expected to solve absorption perfectly. They also stress that toy results are not proofs and may not hold under other co-occurrence assumptions.
record.recipe_differences: The post uses synthetic feature-generating toy settings and compares tied and untied SAEs, capacity regimes, and a custom auxiliary loss. It is not a direct replication of the dictionary-size feature-splitting method.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes differ with dictionary width (overcomplete versus undercomplete), tied versus untied weights, feature co-occurrence, superposition, and use of the custom auxiliary loss.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy tied SAEs, broken latents show multiple activation peaks (4 peaks for latents 0 and 4). A real Gemma-2-2b tied SAE latent also shows multiple peaks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multiple activation-histogram peaks diagnose absorbed or mixed features in SAE latents.

fits_no_version.finding: Tied SAEs keep their learned latents mutually orthogonal even when the latents are broken.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tied SAEs have an orthogonality bias that makes them more resistant to absorption than untied SAEs.

record.problems: The experiments are toy settings rather than tests of true features in language models. The post says the toy settings are not mathematical proofs and that conclusions may not hold under all feature co-occurrence assumptions. The proposed auxiliary loss has not been made to work well on real LLM SAEs; the authors suspect real activation distributions overlap. Several outcomes are described qualitatively rather than numerically.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported numerical or qualitative result on feature magnitudes, firing probabilities, expected MSE rankings, or latent-to-latent cosine plots was included because these do not directly measure the claim versions. Cited studies and results discussed in comments were also left out.

untested.parts: No progression of dictionary sizes producing finer child features near a coarse feature's direction.
No large-model or open-release splitting comparison. The one Gemma latent is anecdotal.
No test of geometric feature families mirroring a concept hierarchy.
Sparsity (L1) was not varied systematically. Untied SAEs with co-occurrence at overcomplete width were not run. Real-LLM absorption was not measured.
No cross-size decomposition or novel-latent analysis.
Matryoshka SAEs were not trained. The argument comes from 1-latent SAEs. The custom loss was not shown to work on real LLMs.

missing.what: Toy activation histograms for broken latents 0 and 4: 4 peaks, weak firing when parent feature 12 is active alone, strong when the child is present. This is evidence of the mixed parent/child encoding.

record.verdict_notes: Toy-only evidence, described qualitatively from figures with no numbers. The author is first author of an original source (A is for Absorption), but this post is a separate study. The independent-feature rows (R1, R2, R4, R5) are controls and were unlinked from V4.

versions.untested_parts: No test of increasing dictionary size producing related, directionally close child features whose inputs partition a coarse feature.
No large-model or open-release comparison of feature splitting across SAE sizes or families.
No test of nested geometrically close feature families mirroring a concept hierarchy.

The post tests whether co-occurrence and narrow dictionaries produce broken parent/child representations, but does not establish the specific firing exception where a parent latent fails whenever a child latent takes over. It does not systematically vary sparsity.
No cross-dictionary decomposition comparison or test for novel latents as dictionary size changes.

Toy experiments compare standard training with a custom activation-orthogonality loss. The post does not directly test Matryoshka SAEs or establish that SAE objectives explain features in trained language models.

relation.reason: It runs its own toy experiments on co-occurrence, SAE width and training objective.

tranche.reason: The post argues that the Matryoshka premise is not strictly true and that tied SAEs break when there are fewer latents than features. That is an argument for restating the versions.

source_check.notes: All results are qualitative (cosine-similarity plots, no numbers). Broken tied cases use 5 latents for 20 features; the clean case uses 8 latents for 4 features; the 1-latent case has 4 features. The post treats latent count relative to feature count as the key variable, and several statements omit it. Untied SAEs were not run on co-occurrence here, except the 1-latent case (R12).

statements.correction: This study: in a tied 5-latent SAE on 20 features, the child latents for 5 and 7 include part of parent 12, and the parent has no latent of its own (R6). The 1-latent untied (R12) and tied (R13) SAEs merge parent 0 with children 1 and 2 in one latent. The authors call these broken latents, not strictly absorption.
statements.problem: This study's R6, R12 and R13 are cited as evidence of a parent latent with a firing hole, but none of them shows one. R6 and R13 are tied SAEs, while the conditions say untied. The authors say the 1-latent cases are not technically absorption, and they doubt that R6 is absorption either.
none. Only a tied SAE was run. Untied SAEs at 8 latents were not tested on co-occurrence.

statements.correction: Tied 5-latent SAE on 20 features, parent 12 or 6 with children 5 and 7: broken latents (R6, R8). Tied 8-latent SAE on 4 features: clean (R3). The post's takeaway is that tied SAEs fail when there are fewer latents than true features.
statements.problem: differences_stated leaves out the difference the post treats as decisive. The broken tied cases have 5 latents for 20 features, fewer latents than features. The clean cases have at least as many latents as features. The post explains the apparent conflict with exactly this.

statements.correction: Narrow toy SAEs (fewer latents than features), tied or untied, mix parent and children. R8: tied 5-latent SAE, features 5, 6 and 7 merged into 2 combo latents. R12/R13: 1-latent untied and tied SAEs merge parent 0 with children 1 and 2.
statements.problem: "Narrow or tied" makes tying alone the condition. In this study a tied SAE with 8 latents for 4 features is clean (R3). All three cited rows are narrow SAEs. Also, R8 merges 3 features into 2 latents, not into one.

statements.correction: Tied, 8 latents for 4 features: clean (R3). Tied, 5 latents for 20 features: broken, both orthogonal (R6, R8) and superposed in 19 dimensions (R10, noisier; features 5, 6 and 7 mixed).
statements.problem: In this study, superposition does not change whether tied SAEs stay clean. The orthogonal 5-latent case is already broken (R6, R8), and superposition only makes it noisier (R10). The post's variable is latent count relative to feature count, not feature count as a data statistic.
none. It omits that these are tied SAEs with 5 latents for 20 features.

statements.correction: Tied 5-latent SAE, 20 features, children 5 and 7: child latents include part of parent 12 (R6). Parent 6 merges with its children into 2 combo latents (R8). Under superposition, features 5, 6 and 7 are mixed (R10). Tied 8-latent SAE, 4 features: clean (R3).
statements.problem: differences_stated omits that the broken cases are tied 5-latent SAEs on 20 features (fewer latents than features). It also omits that the post finds tied SAEs clean at 8 latents for 4 features (R3). The post uses this latent count to reconcile its results with the earlier tied-SAE result.
